judged.summary:
Lens: will a newcomer follow it? I heard each draft once at speaking speed as three first-time viewers who haven't seen chapter 1: S, a 17-year-old student; B, a 60-year-old retired builder who left school at 16; and E, an adult whose first language isn't English. All three drafts are far easier to follow than the recording. None has digits, capitals, brackets, "MMT", banned Klein words or "I". Mattei is always marked as hers. The longest sentence in each is 19 words.

Ranking for "can a newcomer explain the idea and use it on a new case":
1. one-model, 7.5
2. viewer-question, 7
3. people-first, 5.5

one-model wins because it builds the two-factories picture first, says what it stands for ("think of each one as a whole country"), and then places every later case on it out loud. Japan "never reached the factory", the cure makes "the factory slow, more workers wait at the gate", fuel raises "prices in both factories", and Mattei's "those workers at the gate". That gives a viewer a tool they can carry to a new case. Its weak spots are page 10 (homes) and page 13 (prices now). people-first is the most human, but it is the heaviest to take in, it drops the costs idea and it plants "the cure makes prices fall".

Load per 30 seconds. I counted new places, years or dates, numbers and terms, first mention only, tagged by hand. The script turns each tag's word position into seconds at 140 words a minute, with 1.5 s page turns and 3 s guess holds.

| Draft | Running time | Places | Years/dates | Numbers | Terms | All | Average per 30 s | Worst 30 s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| viewer-question | about 6:38 | 3 | 7 | 12 | 19 | 41 | 3.1 | 7, at 0:30 to 1:00 |
| one-model | about 6:45 | 3 | 6 | 13 | 17 | 39 | 2.9 | 6, at 2:30 to 3:00 (Japan plus four numbers) |
| people-first | about 6:35 | 5 | 9 | 17 | 19 | 50 | 3.8 | 8, at 0:30 to 1:00 |

- people-first's worst stretch has four places in about 12 seconds: New Zealand, Glasgow, Scotland, Britain.
- At Malina's measured 164 words a minute, the times are 5:44, 5:50 and 5:41. The averages become 3.6, 3.3 and 4.4, and the worst stretches 8, 7 and 10.
- The audit counted the recording more broadly, so the figures aren't exact equals: about 11 per 30 s, worst 16.
- Average words per sentence: 7.6, 8.8 and 8.8.

Time order:
- one-model runs strictly forward.
- viewer-question runs forward, apart from a small step back to 2021 for the cure.
- people-first jumps back from New Zealand 2021 to Britain 1920, then returns. It says why, but it is still a zigzag.

Reader-comprehension probes (toolkit):
- **Main claim:** all three state the rule in plain words twice. viewer-question and people-first word it as conditions ("if there are spare workers, materials and machines..."). one-model words it with the factory names, which only works because it has mapped the factories to a country.
- **Evidence, inference and qualification:** these are easiest to hear in one-model. "Picture two factories" is followed by "This really happened", and it says "most economists agree", "one reason economists give", "a Royal Commission found... part of the reason", "economists argue" and "she argues".
- **Transfer:** no draft gives the viewer a clue and then asks them to apply the rule. viewer-question's "which factory was New Zealand? Have a guess" (page 10) comes closest, but the clue (3.2 percent unemployment) only comes after the guess. one-model and people-first apply the rule for the viewer.
- **Teaching plan's key question** (new money paying builders): one-model and viewer-question risk the answer "homes always push prices up", because homes are taught as something we can't make more of in a hurry. people-first sets this up best: homes are slow "not with the builders and materials gone to war".
- **Smaller goal**, telling a rise from spending apart from a rise in costs: people-first cut fuel entirely, so its viewers can't do this. viewer-question teaches costs but doesn't place them on the factories. one-model does both.

Not tested: the three listeners are imagined, as in the audit. No real newcomer has heard any draft and Malina hasn't read them, so the timings are estimates.

scores.strengths:
Newcomer say-backs:
- S: "Think of a country as a factory: with workers waiting, new money gets more made; flat out, it pushes prices up. Money that isn't spent doesn't count. Fuel pushes prices up either way. The cure slows the factory, and Mattei says the jobless are the point."
- B: "Spare hands and machines, the money gets used making stuff; everyone flat out, prices go up."
- E: "When all the workers are busy, new money makes prices go up."

Picture and checks:
- Page 3 says what the picture stands for: "Think of each one as a whole country... all its workers, materials and machines."
- Page 4's guess is a real prediction the viewer can reason out from the picture: "The same new money is spent there. What do you think happens?"
- Page 5 is the only draft that hints at why prices rise: "Just more money, offered for the same things... so prices rise."
- Page 6's "This really happened" separates the imagined picture from real evidence.
- Page 7's Japan guess is a real surprise.

Every example's lesson is said aloud and placed on the picture:
- Britain (page 6): "close to the flat-out factory".
- Japan (page 8): "In our picture, it never reached the factory".
- New Zealand (page 9): "Very few workers were spare. That's close to the flat-out factory."
- The cure (page 11): "the factory slows... and more workers wait at the gate".
- Fuel (page 13): "prices rise in both factories... with or without new money".
- Mattei (page 14): "those workers at the gate".

Wording and order:
- Page 9 defines unemployment before giving the number.
- Page 11 says "home loans", not "mortgages".
- Page 12 makes clear the 170,000 is everyone out of work, not the rise: "Five point six percent is about a hundred and seventy thousand people."
- Page 15 repeats page 5's rule word for word.
- Time and place run forward only: Britain, Japan, New Zealand.
- It has the fewest new items overall: 39, about 2.9 every 30 seconds.
scores.faults:
First places each listener gets lost:
- **B:** page 10. "House prices aren't in the shopping basket. But..." is a point about how prices are measured that he can't use. Then "A Royal Commission, an official inquiry, found the economic response to Covid was part of the reason. So were world events." has a definition squeezed mid-sentence, and the abstract "economic response" and "world events" follow it.
- **E:** also lost at page 10 ("inquiry", "response"). Before that, page 1's "Create new money... and prices will rise" reads as an order, and "central bank" is explained only by example.
- **All:** page 13 runs 37 seconds with four numbers in about 15 seconds (4.1, 2.9, one to three, fuel). "pushed the whole basket past that" has an unclear "that", and it ends on a question left hanging ("Can the usual cure fix a rise in costs? Economists argue about that.").

Terms left unexplained:
- "central bank": shown by example only.
- "inquiry" and "economic response to Covid".
- "the usual cure": promised on page 1, explained on page 11, about four minutes later.

Voice-brief breach: page 1 uses "cost" as a figure of speech ("can cost people their jobs").

Transfer risk: page 10's "You can't build a house in a hurry. So money spent on homes mostly pushes prices up... like the flat-out factory" invites "homes always push prices up". A viewer may then fail the builders question.

The rule is worded with the factory names rather than plain conditions, one step removed from a new case. No viewer application check: the narrator applies the picture to New Zealand.

scores.strengths:
Newcomer say-backs:
- S: "New money doesn't always raise prices. With spare workers and machines it mostly gets more made; when everything's busy, prices go up. Japan's money mostly sat in banks. The fix, a higher interest rate, puts people out of work."
- B: "Printing money only drives prices up when there's nobody spare to do the work, like in the war."
- E: "Money makes prices go up when the factories are full."

Pace:
- Easiest to hear: 16 short pages and 7.6 words a sentence, about one new item every 30 seconds (3.1).
- Page 2 says plainly who can create new money (the Reserve Bank) and ends with a memory cue: "Hold on to that."
- Page 1's warning is the clearest for E: "If the government creates new money... prices will go up." Page 1 avoids "cost" as a figure of speech.

Tests and lessons:
- Pages 3 and 4: test one's lesson is said aloud and tied back to page 2: "So far, the warning seems right. But look closer. Britain was short of workers, materials and machines."
- Pages 5 and 6: test two is a guess most viewers will get wrong, then a plain verdict: "So no... new money doesn't always push prices up."
- Page 8 says Britain was "close to the flat-out factory".
- Page 10's test three is the only place in any draft where the viewer is asked to apply the picture to a new case: "A country can be either factory... which factory was New Zealand? Have a guess."

Wording:
- Page 11 gives unemployment example first: "Only about three in every hundred people who wanted a job couldn't find one. That's called unemployment... three point two percent."
- Page 13: "Interest is the extra you pay back when you borrow" and "Not fall... rise more slowly."
scores.faults:
First places each listener gets lost:
- **S:** page 7 opens "So what made the difference?", but page 6 has just answered that (the money sat in the banks). The quiet factory ("more gets made... and prices hardly move") then follows Japan's flat prices, which invites "Japan was the quiet factory". The ledger doesn't support that, and Japan is never placed on the picture.
- **B:** page 6's "Mainstream economists", again on page 9. Then page 12: "If petrol and diesel prices hadn't changed... they'd have risen two point nine... So the fuel part isn't about spending. It's a cost." That is a hard grammatical form for B and E, with no 1 to 3 percent target to tell him whether 2.9 is good or bad.
- **E:** page 5's "Its version of our Reserve Bank" ("its" after a sentence fragment), page 7's "new orders" (orders can mean commands), and page 11's "an independent review said the support... too strong, for too long".

Terms left unexplained:
- "mainstream", twice.
- "independent review".
- "orders", which E may hear as commands.
- "the usual cure": promised on page 1, explained on page 13, about four and a half minutes later.

Mapping and wording problems:
- The factory is said to stand for a country only on page 10.
- Fuel isn't placed on the factories.
- Page 11: "The flat-out one" drops the "close to" used everywhere else.
- No price outcome is given for New Zealand 2021.
- Test three's guess comes before its clue, so it is a guess, not an application.
- Page 14: after "climbed from three point two percent to five point six", "That's a hundred and seventy-one thousand people" can be heard as the rise.
- Page 15: "The people who set interest rates" is a second name for the Reserve Bank.
- Page 9's homes line carries the same "homes always push prices up" risk as one-model.

scores.strengths:
Newcomer say-backs:
- S: "New money mostly makes more stuff when there are spare workers and machines, and pushes prices up when there aren't. Japan's money sat in banks. Raising interest rates in 1920 put more than one in ten out of work."
- B: "In the war nobody was spare, so prices doubled and landlords put the rents up." B relates to the Glasgow homes and families.
- E: keeps the Glasgow story and the rule's first half.

Wording that helps newcomers:
- Page 1 names the cure straight away, so nothing is left hanging: "the usual cure is to make borrowing cost more. And that can put people out of work."
- Page 2 says what the Reserve Bank is: "It's the bank in charge of the country's money."
- It keeps one name throughout: "out of work", never "unemployment". Each foreign bank is "[country]'s version of our Reserve Bank".
- Page 9: "two outside experts reviewed what the Reserve Bank did" is the plainest way any draft gives the review.

Pictures and lessons:
- Page 4 ties the shortage of homes to busy builders: "You can't build homes in a hurry... not with the builders and materials gone to war." That is the right setup for the builders question.
- Page 6 states the rule as plain conditions and repeats it word for word on page 14.
- Page 8's recap says "whether it's spent... and on what".

The most human, in Klein's spirit: real people (Mary Barbour, twenty thousand families) and who gains and who pays side by side (landlords and tenants).

Qualifications are said aloud: "Historians still argue over how much the interest rate caused" and "Not all of that is because of the interest rate."
scores.faults:
First places each listener gets lost:
- **E:** page 3. "Glasgow, in Scotland... nineteen fifteen. Britain is fighting the First World War" gives Glasgow, Scotland, Britain, 1915 and the war in about 10 seconds; E may not know Scotland is in Britain. Then "shells", which E may hear as sea shells, and page 4's "refuse to pay any more", which E may hear as "stop paying anything".
- **B:** page 11. "Not about two in every hundred... but more than one in ten" mixes "in a hundred" and "in ten". Then page 13 repeats the recording's worst habit: two pairs of decimals almost back to back ("from a quarter of a percent... to five and a half percent... from three point two to five point six").

Teaching faults:
- Page 11's "Prices do fall" plants the very misconception the teaching plan said to avoid, and no line says "rise more slowly, not fall" for New Zealand. B leaves thinking the cure makes prices fall.
- Fuel and costs were cut, so its viewers can't tell a rise from spending apart from a rise in costs. That is one of the plan's stated goals.
- Page 4's strike story says its lesson only later, as "And so were Glasgow's homes" on page 6.

Mapping:
- It never says the factory stands for a whole country.
- Japan isn't placed on the picture.
- The cure isn't placed on the picture.

Unexplained or figurative terms:
- "shells".
- "a cost, not the goal": a figurative cost, in a chapter where cost means prices.
- "part of the point": an idiom.
- "wage subsidy", for non-New Zealand ears.

Other:
- The densest draft: 50 new items. The opening minute's worst stretch has 8, and 10 at Malina's real pace.
- Page 13: "That's about a hundred and seventy thousand people" can be heard as the rise.

judged.best_parts_to_keep:
Base: one-model's teaching spine, pages 3 to 15. It is the picture a newcomer can reuse. Graft these in, in order.

Opening:
- people-first page 1: "the usual cure is to make borrowing cost more. And that can put people out of work." It names the cure at once and avoids one-model's figurative "cost people their jobs".
- viewer-question page 1: "If the government creates new money... prices will go up." Clearer for E than "Create new money... and prices will rise".
- people-first page 2: "It's the bank in charge of the country's money." One plain line on what the Reserve Bank is. With it, one-model's "a country's central bank" can go.

The picture and the rule:
- one-model page 3: "Think of each one as a whole country... all its workers, materials and machines."
- one-model page 4: the guess "The same new money is spent there. What do you think happens?" with its 3-second hold.
- one-model page 5: "Just more money, offered for the same things... so prices rise. Most economists agree on this much." Plain "most", not "mainstream".
- viewer-question page 9 or people-first page 6: the rule worded as conditions, "If there are spare workers, materials and machines... new money mostly gets more made. If there aren't... it mostly pushes prices up". Easier to carry to a new case than the factory names alone. Repeat it word for word at the end.

Britain and Japan:
- one-model page 6: "This really happened."
- viewer-question page 4: "So far, the warning seems right. But look closer. Britain was short of workers, materials and machines." It goes with viewer-question page 2's "Hold on to that."
- viewer-question pages 5 and 6: "If the warning is right, prices should rise fast. What happened? Have a guess." and "So no... new money doesn't always push prices up."
- one-model page 8: "In our picture, it never reached the factory. So it isn't just how much new money is created. It's whether it's spent... and what it's spent on."

New Zealand:
- viewer-question page 11: "Only about three in every hundred people who wanted a job couldn't find one. That's called unemployment... three point two percent."
- viewer-question page 10: "A country can be either factory... which factory was New Zealand? Have a guess." Keep it as a real application check, but move the clue (very few workers spare) before the question.
- people-first page 9: "two outside experts reviewed what the Reserve Bank did". Use it if the review line comes back.
- people-first page 4's logic for homes: "You can't build homes in a hurry... not with the builders and materials gone to war." Tie the shortage to busy builders, not to homes as such.

The cure and who pays:
- viewer-question page 13: "Interest is the extra you pay back when you borrow." and "And prices rise more slowly. Not fall... rise more slowly."
- one-model page 11: "In our picture, the factory slows... and more workers wait at the gate."
- one-model page 12: "Five point six percent is about a hundred and seventy thousand people, looking for work." It is clearly everyone out of work, not the rise.
- one-model page 13: "When fuel costs more, prices rise in both factories... with or without new money."
- one-model page 14: "She argues those workers at the gate aren't a side effect. They're how the cure works."

Closing: one-model page 15 or viewer-question page 16, "Spent on what? And who pays to stop it?"
judged.must_fix:
For the draft taken forward (one-model as base):

1. **Page 13, prices now: 37 seconds, the heaviest page.** It has four numbers in about 15 seconds, an unclear "past that", and a question left hanging. Split it into two pages, or drop the one to three percent target together with "Can the usual cure fix a rise in costs? Economists argue about that." If that question goes, page 12's "And this year, the Reserve Bank has raised its interest rate again" must go with it. Its own notes pair them, because of the ledger's "never mostly fuel" warning (C2-M18). Keep the 4.1 and 2.9 tied to the year to June twenty twenty-six. Keep Stats NZ's own wording.

2. **Page 10, homes: lightening and transfer.**
   - Take out the definition squeezed mid-sentence ("A Royal Commission, an official inquiry, found..."). Either give it its own sentence or cut the Royal Commission line.
   - Say "house prices aren't in the shopping basket" in a way B can use, or move it to the screen only. The ledger trap still applies: never put house prices next to the inflation figure.
   - Tie "can't build a house in a hurry" to busy builders and materials, as in people-first page 4. Otherwise viewers learn "homes always push prices up" and fail the builders question. Keep "part of the reason" and the world events (C2-M10, C2-N14) if the line stays.

3. **Page 1.** Name the cure at once ("make borrowing cost more"), and replace "can cost people their jobs" with "can put people out of work". The voice brief bans "cost" as a figure of speech. Use viewer-question's "If the government creates new money... prices will go up" in place of the imperative.

4. **Add one real application check.** Give the clue before the guess (for example, "Very few workers were spare" or the three-in-a-hundred line), then ask "which factory was New Zealand?", as in viewer-question page 10. Use "close to the flat-out factory" in the answer, never a flat "the flat-out one".

5. **Two names for one thing.** Use one plain wording for the bank's role, either "central bank" or the Reserve Bank explained in plain words, not both as separate terms. Never "mainstream", never "the people who set interest rates" as a second name.

If viewer-question is chosen instead:
- Place Japan on the picture ("it never reached the factory").
- Cut "So what made the difference?" after Japan's reason has been given, or move the two factories before Japan.
- Say the factory stands for a whole country on page 7.
- "Mainstream" becomes "most".
- Explain the review ("two outside experts").
- "The flat-out one" becomes "Close to the flat-out one".
- Make the 171,000 clearly the total.
- Rewrite the fuel line for the ear, avoiding "would have... if... hadn't".

If people-first is chosen instead:
- Fix "Prices do fall" with "not fall... rise more slowly" for New Zealand.
- Restore a short costs line from its ready insert.
- Split page 13's back-to-back decimal pairs.
- Thin page 3's place cluster.
- Replace "a cost, not the goal" and "part of the point".

Before recording, whichever draft is chosen: read it aloud to one or two of the people who got lost and ask the builders question. "Prices rose 4.1, and 2.9 without fuel: was that new money?" is the second test. No real newcomer has heard any draft yet.

judged.summary:
I read all three narrations aloud the way Malina would. Lens: voice and sound. All three pass the project's voice checker: no capitals, digits, brackets, exclamation marks or Naomi Klein phrases, Mattei is written /məˈteɪi/ and marked "she argues / she says", and no sentence runs over 19 words. All three put the stakes in the first half-minute and end on the same strong pair: "Spent on what? And who pays to stop it?" They differ in how alive they are and where they trip the tongue.

People-first (7.5) is the most alive and the closest to Klein in spirit. It has a real place and real people (Glasgow 1915, landlords raising rents, twenty thousand families refusing, Mary Barbour, Parliament bringing rents back down). It puts who gains and who pays side by side, ends a story on people winning something, and has the fewest stock bridges and "So" openers (6). Its sound problems sit on two pages: page 13 (seven spoken figures in four sentences, two kinds of percent back to back, and a jump forward to 2023 then back to 2021) and page 11 ("Not about two in every hundred... but more than one in ten"). It also keeps one figurative "cost".

One-model (7) has the best single device in any draft: "workers wait at the gate" comes back as a refrain in the quiet factory, the usual cure and Mattei's argument, which makes who pays something you can see. It falls down on page 1 ("The answer matters", plus a figurative "cost people their jobs") and page 13 (86 words, four figures, an apposition the voice may not mark, ending on "Economists argue about that"). "So were world events" is a limp landing.

Viewer-question (6.5) is the easiest on the tongue, with the shortest sentences (7.6 words on average) and three real guess holds. But it sounds most like a worksheet: eleven sentences start with "So", there are seven canned bridges ("So here's the question", "Hold on to that", "But look closer", "Here's the answer", "Back to the question"), there is no named person or lived scene, and it shows who pays but never who gains.

My recommendation for voice: use people-first as the base. Graft in one-model's "workers at the gate" refrain on the cure and Mattei pages. Replace people-first's page 13 with viewer-question's simpler New Zealand cure: no interest-rate figures, "again and again".

Not tested: Malina hasn't read any draft, and no listener has heard one. My read-aloud is simulated. Timings are the drafters' estimates plus the checker's 140 words a minute. I checked a few voice-driven claims against the ledger but did not do a full fact check. Working files (copied narrations, the project checker, and my sound scanner, which counts figures per sentence, "So" openers, rise/raise clashes, figurative "cost" and stock bridges) are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Music/02fc5154-76f5-5aac-a505-860164e7e921/scratchpad/script-rewrite/work-judge-voice-and-sound. Nothing outside that folder was changed.

scores.strengths: The most urgent and alive draft, in Klein's spirit without her words. It is built from scenes you could film: page 3 is told in the present tense ('Britain is fighting the First World War. Crowds of workers come to make shells for the war'), and page 4 is the best-sounding page in any draft. On page 4 landlords raise the rent 'by up to a quarter', 'The families who rent say no', Mary Barbour leads them, 'about twenty thousand families are refusing', and Parliament brings rents back to before the war. That gives who gains and who pays side by side, plus people winning something, all sourced (C2-XB01, XB02). Page 11 gives the cure step by step, then 'Prices do fall' and a fair 'Historians still argue over how much the interest rate caused.' Mattei is marked twice. It avoids the rise/raise clash by having prices go on 'climbing' (page 10). It has the fewest 'So' openers (6) and the fewest stock bridges. It never shouts or preaches: the force comes from putting facts side by side.
scores.faults: Page 13 is the hardest page to hear in all three drafts. It has seven spoken figures in four sentences ('a quarter of a percent... five and a half percent by twenty twenty-three. Since late twenty twenty-one, the percentage out of work has climbed from three point two to five point six'). Those are two different percentages back to back, the time jumps forward to 2023 and back to 2021, 'the percentage out of work' is a clunky noun phrase, and 'percent' is dropped after the numbers. Then 'That's about a hundred and seventy thousand people' comes straight after the climb, so it can be heard as the size of the rise (the voice brief's trap; it is the total). Page 11: 'Not about two in every hundred... but more than one in ten' sounds like a correction, not a change over time, and the two fractions count out of different totals (a hundred, ten), so the ear can't compare them. Page 12: 'call lost jobs a cost, not the goal' uses 'cost' as a figure of speech, which the brief forbids and which the drafter's notes say was removed. Also, the officials' 'not the goal' has no ledger wording. Page 8: 'So it's not how much new money there is' drops the 'just' the other drafts keep, so it says more than the 'mostly' in C2-XA03 and C2-M09 allows. Page 6: 'Nothing more can be made' is absolute where the chapter's rule says 'mostly'. Page 9 crams Covid, billions, the wage subsidy, three point two, record low, the factory and the review into 80 words (34 seconds). 'New money mostly gets more made' runs four m-sounds together, and 'more made' leaves out what is made.

scores.strengths: The strongest refrain in any draft. 'Workers wait at the gate' (page 3) comes back as 'the factory slows... and more workers wait at the gate' (page 11). On page 14 it becomes 'She argues those workers at the gate aren't a side effect. They're how the cure works.' That makes who pays concrete and keeps Mattei's view clearly hers. It is Klein's move of setting the official reason beside what the policy did, done through a picture rather than a slogan. Good ear lines: 'Just more money, offered for the same things... so prices rise' (page 5) and 'In our picture, it never reached the factory' (page 8). It keeps 'close to the flat-out factory' each time. 'Five point six percent is about a hundred and seventy thousand people' (page 12) makes clear it is the total, not the rise. Its rhythm is calm on the teaching pages and leans in on the who-pays pages, as the brief asks.
scores.faults: Page 1: 'The answer matters' is the stock line the viewer-question drafter cut, and 'can cost people their jobs' uses 'cost' as a figure of speech, which the brief forbids. 'Prices will rise... rising prices' also echoes. Page 13 is the heaviest page in the chapter: 86 words, 37 seconds and four figures (four point one, two point nine, one to three percent). 'So one price tag, fuel, pushed the whole basket past that' is an apposition an AI voice may not mark (it can come out as 'one price tag fuel pushed'), and 'past that' asks the listener to do sums by ear. The page then ends on a question answered with 'Economists argue about that', an honest but deflating shrug. Page 10's 'the economic response to Covid' is an abstract noun phrase, and 'So were world events' is a vague, limp landing. Page 12 has three 'interest rate's in five sentences with no pause, which reads flat. On page 12, 'five point six. Five point six percent' back to back may sound like a re-take. 'This really happened' (page 6) is a stock bridge. Pages 11 and 1 put prices rising next to the bank raising. It shows who pays but never who gains, and it names no real person. At 886 words it is the longest.

scores.strengths: The easiest draft on the tongue: 7.6 words per sentence on average and about 27 spoken figures in all. Three real prediction holds ('Before the answer... have a guess'; 'Which factory was New Zealand? Have a guess') make the viewer an active listener. 'So far, the warning seems right' (page 4) states the other side fairly before turning. 'Test three. This one's ours' brings it home. 'And prices at the checkout lately?' (page 12) is a good callback to the opening. 'And prices rise more slowly. Not fall... rise more slowly' (page 13) is ideal ear-writing. 'Looking for work and not finding it' (page 14) turns the number into people. The New Zealand cure page drops the interest-rate figures ('again and again'), the cleanest of the three versions. It uses the independent review's own words. Its ending ('Does new money always push prices up? No.' then the rule and the two questions) lands.
scores.faults: It sounds more like a worksheet than like urgency. Eleven sentences open with 'So', which becomes a drumbeat on the ear, and there are many canned bridges: 'Getting this right matters', 'So here's the question', 'Hold on to that', 'But look closer', 'Here's the answer', 'Back to the question'. That is the toolkit's canned framing. There is no named person and no lived scene: Britain is a list of conditions ('Factories were busy with war work'). It shows who pays but never who gains. Page 12 ends on 'It's a cost' after 'costs more... costs more': a flat, abstract landing where a newcomer may not take 'a cost' as the name of a second cause. Page 5: 'Its version of our Reserve Bank' opens with a word the ear hears as 'It's', a brief stumble ('Japan's version' is clearer). Page 13: 'When prices rise too fast, the Reserve Bank raises its interest rate' puts rise and raises in one sentence. Page 14: 'That's a hundred and seventy-one thousand people' comes straight after 'climbed from three point two percent to five point six', so it can be heard as the rise. combined.how_it_teaches:
Source: Clara E. Mattei, The Capital Order (2022). The base is the one-model draft, which the judges rated best for newcomers. Lines are taken from the viewer-question and people-first drafts, and every must-fix from the three judges is applied.

THE SENTENCE A VIEWER SHOULD BE ABLE TO SAY BACK: whether new money pushes prices up depends on what it's spent on. When there are spare workers, materials and machines, it mostly gets more things made. When there aren't, it mostly pushes prices up. And the usual cure is paid for by people with loans and people out of work.

THE MODEL: one picture comes before any real case. It is two factories, each standing for "a whole country... all its workers, materials and machines".
- The quiet factory: machines still, workers waiting at the gate.
- The flat-out factory: every worker and machine already "working as hard as they can".
- New money is "spent on what it makes", so money that is never spent never reaches the factory.
The rule is said as plain conditions on page 5 and again, word for word, on page 15.

THE CASES (three countries, time running forward), each placed on the picture out loud:
- Britain at war: "close to the flat-out factory".
- Glasgow's homes: "worked like the flat-out factory too", tied to "builders and materials gone to the war". This shows who gains and who pays: landlords raised the rent, about twenty thousand families refused the extra and won.
- Japan 2013: "most of it never reached the factory".
- New Zealand 2020-21: a real application check, with the clue before the question. The answer is "Close to the flat-out factory".
- The usual cure: "the factory slows... and more workers wait at the gate". Prices "go up more slowly. Not down".
- Who pays here: loans, and about 170,000 people out of work by the middle of 2026. "The interest rate isn't the only reason for that."
- The banks' view gets one fair line ("unfortunate... but not the goal"), then Mattei's: "She argues", "she says".
- Fuel at the checkout: "prices go up in both factories... new money or not". That is a rise in costs, not in spending.

GUESSES AND RECAPS:
- Three guesses, each at the end of a page with a 3-second hold: the flat-out factory, Japan, New Zealand.
- The rule is said twice in the same words.
- "Whether it's spent... and on what" follows Japan.
- It closes on "Spent on what? And who pays to stop it?"

ONE NAME FOR EACH THING: "out of work" (never "unemployment"); "the Reserve Bank" (never "central bank"; other banks are "Japan's version of our Reserve Bank" and "banks like our Reserve Bank"); "interest rate" (interest is "the extra you pay back when you borrow"); and prices always "go up", so they never share a sentence with the bank that "raises".

FOR THE EAR:
- About 24 spoken figures, against about 37 in the recording.
- Sentences average about 9 words; the longest is 19.
- The voice checker flagged nothing (no never-use words, capitals, digits, brackets or exclamation marks); /məˈteɪi/ is marked "she argues".
- The sound scan found no rise/raise clash and no figurative "cost".

CUT OR MOVED TO LATER CHAPTERS:
- Bank of England after 2008;
- Germany 1923;
- oil in 1973;
- Britain 1920;
- New Zealand house prices and the Royal Commission;
- the 0.25% to 5.5% figures, the 3.2% to 5.6% pair and the 2026 rate rises;
- the 1-3% target;
- the independent review's "too strong, for too long", cut for length. It is the first line to bring back; its text is ready in the file.

pages.name: The question
pages.text: You've felt it at the checkout. The same basket of shopping costs more than it did a year ago. That's inflation... prices in general, going up. Not one price tag. The whole basket. You've heard the warning too. If the government creates new money... prices will go up. Is that always true? It matters... because when prices go up too fast, the usual cure makes borrowing cost more. And that can put people out of work.
terms_explained: inflation (prices in general, going up; not one price tag, the whole basket)
the usual cure (makes borrowing cost more; explained in full on page 11)
pages.pictures: page-1 reused with its two parts swapped (code only). First the painted checkout: basket on the belt, and the tag going from A YEAR AGO to NOW, labelled EXAMPLE PRICES. Then INFLATION / PRICES IN GENERAL, GOING UP; one tag swings alone, then every tag flips: THE WHOLE BASKET. Then the debating chamber: the invented politician (no party colours) mouths NEW MONEY → PRICES UP?, then IS THAT ALWAYS TRUE?, then BORROWING COSTS MORE → OUT OF WORK. Remove the brass-shell bridge to the old shell-factory page.

pages.name: Where new money comes from
pages.text: Where does new money come from? Here, the Reserve Bank can create it. Economists who study how modern money works say a country like ours can't run out of its own money. What it can run out of... is workers, materials and machines.

economists who study how modern money works (their view, said as theirs)
workers, materials and machines (the real limit)

A card CAN'T RUN OUT OF ITS OWN MONEY / CAN RUN OUT OF..., then page-3's three painted cut-outs (a worker, materials, a lathe) pop up: WORKERS / MATERIALS / MACHINES.

pages.name: The quiet factory
pages.text: Picture two factories. Think of each one as a whole country... all its workers, materials and machines. In the first, the machines stand still. Workers wait at the gate, hoping for a job. Call it the quiet factory. Now new money is spent on what it makes. The workers go in. The machines start. More things get made... and prices barely move.

the quiet factory (machines still, workers waiting at the gate)
new money spent on what the factory makes
pages.pictures: page-3's two-factories Blender set, works A (code only). Cards A WHOLE COUNTRY: WORKERS, MATERIALS, MACHINES and THE QUIET FACTORY. The queue at the gate; coins rain into the yard (NEW MONEY SPENT); the workers go in, the windows light, smoke rises and goods come out. The price counter stays put; its £ sign becomes a plain PRICES label.

pages.name: The flat-out factory (guess 1)
pages.text: In the second factory, every worker and every machine is already busy... working as hard as they can. No one waits at the gate. Call it the flat-out factory. The same new money is spent on what it makes. What do you think happens? Have a guess.

pages.name: The rule
pages.text: No spare workers, materials or machines... so no more things get made. Just more money, offered for the same things... and prices go up. Most economists agree on this much. So when there are spare workers, materials and machines... new money mostly gets more things made. When there aren't... it mostly pushes prices up.

pages.name: Britain at war
pages.text: Now a real case. Britain, during the First World War. Fewer than one worker in a hundred was out of work. German submarines sank ships carrying food and materials. And the war was paid for partly with new money. More money... and fewer things to buy. By the end of the war, prices had roughly doubled. Britain at war was close to the flat-out factory.

pages.name: Glasgow's homes
pages.text: Homes worked like the flat-out factory too. Early in the war, crowds of war workers came to Glasgow, a British city. With builders and materials gone to the war, few new homes were built. So landlords raised the rent... in places by up to a quarter. By November, about twenty thousand families were refusing to pay the extra. Within weeks, Britain's Parliament brought rents on small homes back to what they were before the war.

pages.name: Japan, the guess (guess 2)
pages.text: Japan, twenty thirteen. Japan's version of our Reserve Bank set out to double the money it had created... in two years. If the warning is right, prices should go up fast. What do you think happened? Have a guess.

pages.name: Japan, the answer
pages.text: Prices barely moved. For about eight years, they went up about half a percent a year, on average. Why? One reason economists give... most of the new money just sat in the banks. In our picture, most of it never reached the factory. So it's not just how much new money there is. It's whether it's spent... and on what.

pages.name: New Zealand, the guess (guess 3, an application check)
pages.text: Now, here. When Covid hit in twenty twenty, the Reserve Bank created new money... and the government spent more. By the end of twenty twenty-one, almost everyone who wanted a job had one. Only about three in a hundred were out of work... the lowest since records began. Which factory was New Zealand closer to? Have a guess.

Then a wide shot of both factory models with WHICH ONE?, held about 3 seconds. Drop the card house, +30% and the review desk.

pages.name: The usual cure
pages.text: Close to the flat-out factory. So what's the usual cure, when prices go up too fast? The Reserve Bank raises its interest rate. Interest is the extra you pay back when you borrow. Many loans cost more... so people have less to spend. Businesses sell less, and hire fewer people. And prices go up more slowly. Not down... just more slowly. In our picture, the factory slows... and more workers wait at the gate.

the usual cure, in full

pages.name: Who pays, here
pages.text: Who pays for the cure? From late twenty twenty-one, the Reserve Bank raised its interest rate again and again. Loans cost more, and jobs got harder to find. By the middle of twenty twenty-six, about a hundred and seventy thousand people were out of work. The interest rate isn't the only reason for that.

pages.name: Two views
pages.text: Banks like our Reserve Bank see putting people out of work as unfortunate... but not the goal. The economist Clara E. /məˈteɪi/, whose book this series follows, disagrees. She argues that putting people out of work is how the cure works. With more people at the gate, she says, the workers inside have less power to ask for more pay.

pages.name: Back at the checkout (costs)
pages.text: And the checkout? In the year to June twenty twenty-six, prices here went up four point one percent. Without the rise in petrol and diesel... two point nine. When fuel like that costs more, almost everything that's made or moved costs more. So prices go up in both factories... new money or not. That's a rise in costs... not in spending.

pages.name: Spent on what?
pages.text: Does new money always push prices up? No. When there are spare workers, materials and machines... new money mostly gets more things made. When there aren't... it mostly pushes prices up. So next time you hear the warning... ask two questions. Spent on what? And who pays to stop it?

findings.quote: Spent on what?
findings.problem: The closing question, the line viewers are meant to keep, is never taught. The "on what" half first appears on page 9 ("It's whether it's spent... and on what"), but no case compares two things the money could be spent on. Glasgow is never labelled as an "on what" example. The factory stands for a whole country, which has no "what" to choose between. In the simulation, the student heard it as "what they buy, like hospitals or a war". The listener whose first language isn't English heard "good things or bad things". Only the builder linked it to whether builders are free. In a series about austerity, the bare question sounds like a question about values, not about spare workers, materials and machines. So viewers can leave with the wrong rule.
findings.fix:
Make the question carry the rule, in the same words both times.
- Page 9: "It's whether it's spent... and on what. On things there are spare workers, materials and machines to make... or not."
- Page 15: "Spent on what... and are there spare workers, materials and machines to make it?"
- Give one real "on what" case. The best is New Zealand in 2022, using ledger C2-N02 (Stats NZ: the rise was "driven mainly by construction of new homes and rents"). It links Glasgow's homes to New Zealand's homes and on to the hospitals transfer question.

findings.quote: Close to the flat-out factory. So what's the usual cure, when prices go up too fast?
findings.problem: New Zealand's outcome is never said. The listener hears that almost everyone had a job, and then "So what's the usual cure, when prices go up too fast?". The step "and prices went up fast" is left for the listener to fill in. The student asked "did prices go up here?". Without it, the home case only shows how to sort a country into a factory. It never shows the rule working. The answer also comes with no reason and no pause, and then the densest page begins. That page has seven steps in about 32 seconds, and the listener whose first language isn't English needed it again.
findings.fix:
After the answer, add the reason and the outcome:
"Close to the flat-out factory. Almost no one was waiting at the gate. By the middle of twenty twenty-two, prices here were going up seven point three percent a year... the fastest in thirty-two years." (C2-N01)
- Optionally add: "Mostly from building new homes, and rents." (C2-N02)
- Think about putting these lines on their own short page, so page 11 starts at the cure.

findings.quote: Where does new money come from? Here, the Reserve Bank can create it.
findings.problem:
The Reserve Bank is the main actor in the chapter, but it is never introduced.
- Page 1's warning names "the government", page 2 names the Reserve Bank, and page 10 has both. The student assumed they were the same thing.
- "Japan's version of our Reserve Bank" (page 8) and "Banks like our Reserve Bank" (page 13) only work if the viewer already knows what ours does.
- The listener whose first language isn't English knows a central bank from home, but not this name.
- "Here" can be heard as "Here's the answer" rather than "in New Zealand".
findings.fix:
"In New Zealand, it's the Reserve Bank... the bank whose job is to stop prices going up too fast. It can create new money."
- This is supported by C2-M15 (inflation targeting began here around 1990).
- It also names the actor behind page 1's "usual cure".

findings.quote: Economists who study how modern money works say a country like ours can't run out of its own money. What it can run out of... is workers, materials and machines.
findings.problem:
This is the hardest idea in the chapter, and it gets about 18 seconds and the longest sentence (19 words).
- "A country like ours" and "its own money" carry the key condition without explaining it. In C2-M12 the condition is a country that borrows in its own currency. The listener hears "rich" or "like New Zealand".
- The unnamed group sounds like the whole profession. The ledger marks this as one school's view, and it has critics.
- The student and the builder both stalled on "then why can't the government pay for everything?".
- The sentence that starts "What it can run out of" made the listener whose first language isn't English replay it.
findings.fix:
"Some economists, who study how modern money works, say a country that makes its own money, like ours, can't run out of it. But it can run out of workers, materials and machines."
- "Some" shows it is a view, not settled fact. The wording still never names the school.

findings.quote: When Covid hit in twenty twenty, the Reserve Bank created new money... and the government spent more.
findings.problem: Japan has just taught that most of its new money "never reached the factory". Nothing then says why New Zealand's would. The listener assumes the Reserve Bank's new money was spent this time. The student asked "why was ours spent and Japan's not?". The ledger is weaker than that assumption. C2-N06 says the money created here also "sits as bank reserves", and economists argue over how much reached spending. The builder also wanted to know what the money was spent on, and the script never says.
findings.fix:
Make the spending that was clearly spent the government's spending, and say what it was spent on:
"...and the government spent much more... including paying wages so people could keep their jobs." (C2-N14: wage subsidies supported over a million workers)
- Don't imply the Reserve Bank's own new money is what got spent.
- Have a fact checker confirm the contrast wording.

findings.quote: She argues that putting people out of work is how the cure works. With more people at the gate, she says, the workers inside have less power to ask for more pay.
findings.problem: The two views sound the same to a newcomer. Page 11 has already said the cure works by making businesses hire fewer people, so "how the cure works" sounds like agreement. Mattei's last sentence then stops before it gets back to prices. The student asked "so what if workers can't ask for more pay... how does that slow prices?".
findings.fix:
Make the two mechanisms visibly different, and finish her chain.
- Banks: "Banks like ours say the cure works by cutting spending... job losses are unfortunate, but not the goal." (C2-M17, C2-XD01)
- Mattei: "...less power to ask for more pay. Pay rises get the blame for prices going up, she says... so the cure works by holding pay down." (C2-H18; keep it said as hers)

findings.quote: By the middle of twenty twenty-six, about a hundred and seventy thousand people were out of work.
findings.problem: Page 10 counted people out of work as "three in a hundred". Page 12 switches to a total, so no listener could tell how much worse things got. The builder asked "out of how many?". A big number is also hard to catch by ear for the listener whose first language isn't English. "Raised its interest rate again and again" sounds as if it went on until 2026. That makes "isn't the only reason" hard to understand. In fact the rate was cut from August 2024 (C2-N10, C2-XD05).
findings.fix:
Use the same unit as page 10, and date the rises:
"From late twenty twenty-one to the middle of twenty twenty-three, the Reserve Bank raised its interest rate again and again... By the middle of twenty twenty-six, nearly six in a hundred were out of work... the most in about ten years." (C2-N10, C2-XD05: 5.6%, highest since 2015)
- Swap the total for this rather than adding to it.
- Relabel the on-screen card to match.

findings.quote: That's a rise in costs... not in spending.
findings.problem: Throughout the script, "costs more" has meant the shop price ("the basket costs more") or the price of a loan ("loans cost more"). So "a rise in costs" is heard as "prices went up", and the contrast is lost. "Spending" is a new name at minute six. Two lines earlier, "Without the rise in petrol and diesel... two point nine" drops both the verb and "percent". The listener whose first language isn't English and the builder both lost the second figure. Nothing tells the listener whether four point one counts as "too fast".
findings.fix:
"Without the rise in petrol and diesel, they'd have gone up two point nine percent." (C2-N05)
"That's a rise in what it costs to make and move things... not new money being spent."
- This keeps the existing names "new money" and "spent".

findings.quote: More money... and fewer things to buy.
findings.problem: There is a near miss the script never separates. Britain's sunk ships (fewer things, caused from outside) are filed under "close to the flat-out factory". Page 14's fuel rise (also from outside) is filed as "a rise in costs" that hits "both factories". On a drought case with no new money, the simulated listeners split between "flat-out factory, like the sunk ships" and "a rise in costs".
findings.fix: On page 6, name both pushes: "Two things pushed prices up at once... more money, and fewer things to buy." On page 14, point back to it: the fuel rise is the second kind of push, the kind the sunk ships were. Have a fact checker review the wording against C2-XA01/XA02, which I did not open.

findings.quote: Homes worked like the flat-out factory too.
findings.problem:
Four problems:
- The factory picture silently changes from "a whole country" to "one kind of thing".
- There is no new money in this story, so the student asked "what's this got to do with new money?".
- The ending (Parliament brought rents back) has no stated point, so listeners didn't know why the story stops there or who gained and who paid.
- The listener whose first language isn't English was thrown by "Homes worked".
findings.fix: Open with: "A factory can also stand for one kind of thing... like homes." Close with who gained and who paid: "Landlords gained. Families paid... until they refused, and won." This also prepares the viewer for "spent on what".

findings.quote: And who pays to stop it?
findings.problem: "It" could mean the warning, the new money, or prices going up. "Pays" has meant rent, paying back a loan and wages earlier in the script. Here it is used in a figurative sense, and the listener whose first language isn't English heard "who gives money to stop it".
findings.fix: Reuse page 12's exact words: "And who pays for the cure?"

findings.quote: Now new money is spent on what it makes.
findings.problem: "It" can point back to "new money", which is the subject of the same sentence: money spent on what the money makes. The listener whose first language isn't English took it that way. The sentence also hides who spends. It is the core action of the picture and is said twice (again on page 4).
findings.fix: "Now new money is spent buying what the factory makes." On page 4: "The same new money is spent buying what this factory makes."

findings.quote: Call it the flat-out factory.
findings.problem: The builder and the student know "flat out". For a listener whose first language isn't English, "flat" can mean unchanging ("prices stayed flat"), which is the opposite meaning. In New Zealand it can also mean a rented home. Japan's picture is an almost flat line. The meaning given just before the name helps.
findings.fix: Keep the name. Put the meaning on screen with it (FLAT OUT = WORKING AS HARD AS THEY CAN). Never use the word "flat" on Japan's line.

findings.quote: When there aren't... it mostly pushes prices up.
findings.problem: The listener has to fill in what "aren't" refers to across a pause. The listener whose first language isn't English lost it the first time (it is repeated on page 15).
findings.fix: "When there aren't any spare...". Change it the same way on both pages so the rule stays word for word.

findings.quote: Banks like our Reserve Bank see putting people out of work as unfortunate... but not the goal.
findings.problem: By ear, "Banks like our Reserve Bank" first sounds like "banks are fond of our Reserve Bank". The listener whose first language isn't English took it that way before recovering.
findings.fix: "Our Reserve Bank, and banks like it, see..."

findings.quote: In our picture, the factory slows... and more workers wait at the gate.
findings.problem: After "two factories", "the factory" doesn't say which one. The listener has to work out that the flat-out factory is slowing.
findings.fix: "In our picture, the flat-out factory slows... and more workers wait at the gate."

findings.quote: One reason economists give... most of the new money just sat in the banks.
findings.problem: The builder asked "why make it if it just sits there?", and nothing answers that. On page 8, "the money it had created" was heard as "all of Japan's money". That doesn't hurt the lesson, but it is vague.
findings.fix: This is acceptable as it stands, since it is honestly given as "one reason". Optionally, on page 8: "set out to double, in two years, all the money it had created" (C2-XB03).

findings.quote: the usual cure makes borrowing cost more. And that can put people out of work.
findings.problem: The listener has to carry this link unexplained for about four minutes until page 11. It works as a hook, but page 11 explains it with different words ("loans cost more", not "borrowing"), so the answer is not clearly heard as the payoff.
findings.fix: Use one name. Either say "makes loans cost more" on page 1, or say "borrowing costs more" on pages 11-12.

findings.quote: So landlords raised the rent... in places by up to a quarter. By November, about twenty thousand families were refusing to pay the extra.
findings.problem: "By up to a quarter" and "By November" (no year) were hard for the listener whose first language isn't English. The on-screen +25% helps only if they are watching.
findings.fix: Keep the +25% card in sync with the words. Optionally say "in places, a quarter more".

findings.quote: What do you think happens? Have a guess.
findings.problem: Three seconds was short for the listener whose first language isn't English to form a guess. This applies to the guesses on pages 4, 8 and 10.
findings.fix: Hold for about 4 seconds, or put a small on-screen marker that the video is waiting for a guess.

I checked every factual sentence on all 15 pages, plus the numbers planned for the screen, against the ledger entries each page cites. I read each entry's claim, plain version, confidence and notes, as well as the 12 October second fact check and the Traps. Most lines hold: Britain's prices roughly doubling, the submarines, "partly with new money", Glasgow's "up to a quarter", "about twenty thousand families", "refusing to pay the extra" and "within weeks", Japan's doubling and "about half a percent", the usual cure step by step, the 170,000 total with its date, the 4.1 and 2.9 with Stats NZ's petrol-and-diesel wording, and Mattei marked as hers twice.

Four must-fixes:
(1) The rule on pages 5 and 15 says "new money mostly gets more things made". The ledger (C2-XA03) is about extra spending, and the script's own Japan page shows new money that sat in the banks and got nothing made.
(2) Page 10's "lowest since records began" has lost the 1986 qualification. The 12 October check had put LOWEST SINCE 1986 on screen because older counts show New Zealand had almost no unemployment in the 1950s to 70s. The combined script took that off the screen and doesn't say it either, though the helpers' plan had it.
(3) Page 11 goes from "close to the flat-out factory" straight to the cure for prices going up too fast. A newcomer will take it that New Zealand's 2021-22 price rise came from the economy running flat out. The ledger (C2-N16) says no one has split that rise, and world prices such as oil were a big part.
(4) Page 14's "That's a rise in costs... not in spending", which answers "And the checkout?", will be heard as the whole 4.1 percent. That is the C2-M18 "mostly fuel" trap in other words. The listener test's question 4 expects that same wrong answer.

Should-fixes:
- Page 2 answers "where does new money come from" with only the Reserve Bank. Most new money is made by ordinary banks lending.
- Page 2 says "a country" can't run out of its own money. The view is about a government that issues it.
- Page 6 says fewer than one in a hundred were out of work throughout the war. The entry only supports "fell below".
- Page 7 drops "homes were already short".
- Page 11's New Zealand answer is the review's judgement but is said in the narrator's voice.
- Page 13's "how the cure works" doesn't clash with the banks' view. Mattei's claim is that putting people out of work is the main aim.
- Page 14's figures will be replaced on 22 October.

Every fix is a few words. Together they add about 40 to 70 words, so they will use up the ready cuts. My work folder is /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Music/02fc5154-76f5-5aac-a505-860164e7e921/scratchpad/script-rewrite/work-test-facts. Nothing outside it was changed, and there are no files in it.

findings.quote: So when there are spare workers, materials and machines... new money mostly gets more things made. When there aren't... it mostly pushes prices up.
findings.problem: This claims more than the entry. C2-XA03's plain version is about extra spending ("With idle workers and machines, extra spending mostly raises output"). It says nothing about new money as such. The script's own Japan case (page 9, C2-C06, C2-XB03) had spare workers and machines (weak demand), doubled its new money, and most of it "just sat in the banks". So new money did not mostly get more things made there. The rule as worded is the sentence viewers are meant to remember, and the film's own evidence contradicts it.
findings.fix: Say "new money that's spent": "So when there are spare workers, materials and machines... new money that's spent mostly gets more things made. When there aren't... it mostly pushes prices up." Make the same change on page 15 so the two stay word for word. Add IF SPENT to the rule cards on screen.

findings.quote: Does new money always push prices up? No. When there are spare workers, materials and machines... new money mostly gets more things made.
findings.problem: This repeats page 5's rule straight after the Japan pages, where new money was created with spare capacity and mostly sat in the banks. As worded, the closing rule is stronger than C2-XA03 (which is about extra spending) and contradicts page 9.
findings.fix: "When there are spare workers, materials and machines... new money that's spent mostly gets more things made. When there aren't... it mostly pushes prices up." This matches the fixed page 5.

findings.quote: Only about three in a hundred were out of work... the lowest since records began.
findings.problem: The qualification has been dropped. C2-N09's note says "'Lowest ever recorded' means since the series began in 1986". The 12 October final reviewer warned that older official counts show New Zealand had almost no unemployment in the 1950s to early 1970s, so "viewers who remember that era could call this wrong". That check changed the screen to LOWEST SINCE 1986. The combined script removes 1986 from the screen (LOWEST SINCE RECORDS BEGAN) and doesn't say it either, so the correction has been undone. The helpers' plan (understanding.md) had "since records began in nineteen eighty-six".
findings.fix: Narration: "...the lowest since this count began, in nineteen eighty-six." Screen: LOWEST SINCE 1986, as the 12 October check set. If one less figure is wanted, say "the lowest in more than thirty years" (screen: LOWEST IN 30+ YEARS). Either is supported by C2-N09.

findings.quote: Close to the flat-out factory. So what's the usual cure, when prices go up too fast?
findings.problem: This states a cause by implication where the ledger supports less. The script never says that New Zealand's prices went up in 2021-22, or why. It goes from "close to the flat-out factory" with "So" to the cure for prices going up too fast, and then to the rate rises from late 2021. A newcomer applying the model will conclude that New Zealand's price rise came from the economy running flat out. Ledger C2-N16 says no published estimate splits it between government spending, Reserve Bank money and world prices, with "evidence on both sides": imported prices rose 8.2 percent against 6.6 percent for home-grown at the end of 2022 (C2-N03), and petrol rose 32 percent and diesel 74 percent in the year to June 2022 (C2-N02). Page 14's costs lesson is only about 2026, so the film ends up teaching "2021-22 was spending, 2026 is costs".
findings.fix: After "Close to the flat-out factory." add: "And prices here went up fast... partly from that, and partly from world prices, like oil." Cite C2-N01 (fastest in thirty-two years), C2-N16 and C2-N02/C2-N03. The next line, "So what's the usual cure, when prices go up too fast?", then follows on. About 15 words.

findings.quote: So prices go up in both factories... new money or not. That's a rise in costs... not in spending.
findings.problem: This page answers "And the checkout?", the film's opening question, and its last line will be heard as the reason for the whole 4.1 percent. That is the C2-M18 trap in other words: fuel adds about 1.2 of the 4.1 points, and prices without petrol and diesel still rose 2.9 percent. The ledger gives no cause for that 2.9 percent, and it does not say the 2026 rise was "not in spending" (C2-N05: cause not researched; C2-M04: one bank's attribution, seen in search only). The file's listener test question 4 ("Was that new money? If they say yes, page 14 is too fast") expects viewers to conclude the whole rise wasn't new money, which the ledger doesn't support.
findings.fix: Narration: "The fuel part is a rise in costs... not in spending." Screen card: THE FUEL PART: A RISE IN COSTS. Change listener test question 4 to "Was the fuel part of that rise caused by new money?"

findings.quote: Where does new money come from? Here, the Reserve Bank can create it.
findings.problem: The ledger supports less than the answer implies. Asked as a question and answered with only the Reserve Bank, it teaches that the Reserve Bank is where new money comes from. C2-M15 says most money is created by ordinary banks making loans, and the page's own research note admits this ("can"), but the narration doesn't. Page 1's warning also says "the government creates new money".
findings.fix: Change the question so the answer isn't heard as the only source: "Who can create new money? Here, the Reserve Bank can." Rename the page "Who can create new money".

findings.quote: Economists who study how modern money works say a country like ours can't run out of its own money.
findings.problem: This shifts the view's subject. C2-M12's plain version is "A government that issues its own money can't run out of it", and it applies only to countries that borrow in their own currency. "A country" includes its households and businesses, which certainly can run out of money, so a newcomer hears a claim the economists don't make.
findings.fix: "Economists who study how modern money works say a government like ours can't run out of the money it issues." The next line then becomes "What it can run out of...", which still works.

findings.quote: Britain, during the First World War. Fewer than one worker in a hundred was out of work.
findings.problem: This is stronger than the entry. C2-H02 gives annual figures under one percent only for 1915 to 1918 (3.16 percent in 1914), and its plain version says it "fell below one in a hundred". The 12 October check found early-1915 months slightly above one percent and called "under 1%" for 1915 right "but only just". "During the war... was" says throughout the war. The entry's reason ("millions were in uniform") is also dropped, though it is what makes workers not spare.
findings.fix: "Britain, during the First World War. With millions in uniform, fewer than one worker in a hundred was soon out of work." Keep the screen card FEWER THAN 1 IN 100 OUT OF WORK.

findings.quote: Early in the war, crowds of war workers came to Glasgow, a British city. With builders and materials gone to the war, few new homes were built.
findings.problem: The entry's qualification is dropped and the cause narrowed. C2-XB01 says the influx was "exacerbating an already acute ... housing crisis", and its plain version says "where homes were already short". The 12 October check adds that Glasgow house building had already slumped before 1914. The script makes the war's pull on builders and materials the only reason homes were short, which also rests on a quote the checker saw second-hand in search results only (Merrett and Sykes). The helpers' plan had "where homes are already short".
findings.fix: "Early in the war, crowds of war workers came to Glasgow, a British city, where homes were already short. And with builders and materials gone to the war, few new homes were built." About 6 words more.

findings.quote: Close to the flat-out factory.
findings.problem: The New Zealand answer is the independent review's judgement, said in the narrator's voice. With the review line cut, nothing on the page backs it except 3.2 percent. C2-N09's note says calling 3.2 percent "unsustainable" is the review's judgement and that "others would see a tight labour market as a good outcome". C2-N15 ("overheated", money from the Reserve Bank's bond buying "later contributed to excess demand") is a government-commissioned review, released in an election year. C2-N06's note also says the Reserve Bank's new money sat as bank reserves and "economists argue over how much this reaches spending". That is the very thing page 9 taught about Japan, and the page leaves it unanswered.
findings.fix: Bring back the review line already drafted in combined.md, shortened, straight after the answer: "Looking back, two outside experts said the new money and the extra government spending were right at first... but too strong, for too long." Keep "looking back" and keep it away from house prices (C2-N15, C2-XC04). Pay for it from the four ready cuts.

findings.quote: disagrees. She argues that putting people out of work is how the cure works.
findings.problem: Mattei's claim is understated, so the two views don't actually clash. The banks' own account also says the cure works partly through fewer jobs (C2-M17: Powell, "softening of labor market conditions", "some pain"). They deny it is the goal, not that it happens. Mattei's claim in the ledger is about the aim: "The main objective of interest rate hikes is to cool down the labor market" and "unemployment serves as the best disciplinary device to suppress wages" (C2-H18). Some newcomers will hear "disagrees" and not know what she disagrees about.
findings.fix: "She argues that putting people out of work is the main aim of the cure." Keep the next sentence, with "she says", unchanged. Screen: MATTEI ARGUES: THE MAIN AIM. It stays marked as hers (C2-H18).

findings.quote: In the year to June twenty twenty-six, prices here went up four point one percent.
findings.problem: This figure goes out of date soon. The September-quarter price figures come out on 22 October 2026, seven days from now (C2-N05, C2-XA05, C2-XC05). Tied to the June year, the line stays true, but it will no longer answer "And the checkout?" for a viewer. Page 1's "costs more than it did a year ago" also rests on it. Page 14's lesson needs a visible gap between prices with and without petrol and diesel, and the new figures may not show one.
findings.fix: Before recording or publishing after 22 October, add the September figures to the ledger first. Then either switch to them, keeping Stats NZ's petrol-and-diesel wording, or keep the June year as worded. Never write "mostly fuel".

findings.quote: If the warning is right, prices should go up fast.
findings.problem: This leaves out context in C2-C06 and C2-C07. Japan's Bank was trying to push prices up, aiming for 2 percent a year within about two years, after about fifteen years of falling prices. Without that, a newcomer may think the Bank feared price rises and escaped them by luck. With it, the point is stronger: even trying, it fell short.
findings.fix: Optional, if there is room: "It even wanted prices to go up. If the warning is right, they should go up fast." No figure is needed.

findings.quote: By the end of twenty twenty-one, almost everyone who wanted a job had one.
findings.problem: This goes a little beyond the entry. The 3.2 percent (C2-N09) counts people without a job who are looking for one. People who want a job but aren't looking aren't in it, so "wanted" is broader than the ledger supports.
findings.fix: "By the end of twenty twenty-one, almost everyone looking for work had a job."

findings.quote: By the middle of twenty twenty-six, about a hundred and seventy thousand people were out of work.
findings.problem: There are two small risks. (1) The 171,000 is from the June 2026 quarter's adjusted series (C2-XD05), and that series gets revised at the next release on 4 November, as March's figure was. (2) Under "Who pays for the cure?" the whole 170,000 can be heard as the cure's toll, though about three in a hundred were out of work even at the 2021 low (C2-N09), and the rise went on while the rate was being cut (C2-XD05). "The interest rate isn't the only reason for that" covers this, so it is acceptable.
findings.fix: After 4 November, re-check that the June-quarter count is still about 170,000. Never cut "The interest rate isn't the only reason for that."

findings.quote: And prices go up more slowly. Not down... just more slowly.
findings.problem: A qualification is dropped. The cure works with a delay: its biggest effect comes after one to two years (C2-M17, RBA), and C2-XD01's note says "It works with a lag". This isn't wrong as it stands, but page 12 then puts the 2021-23 rises next to 2026 jobs without saying the effects take time.
findings.fix: Optional: "And, after a year or two, prices go up more slowly." Or leave it, since nothing on the page claims a speed.

findings.quote: Within weeks, Britain's Parliament brought rents on small homes back to what they were before the war.
findings.problem: The narration is correct (C2-XB02). But the file's description says the families "refused the extra and won", and C2-XB02 notes the law was meant to be temporary and was weakened after 1915. If "won" reaches the screen or a caption, it is stronger than the entry.
findings.fix: Keep the narration. Keep the screen stamp as RENTS BACK TO BEFORE THE WAR and never write WON. In the file's description, change "and won" to "and rents were brought back down".

findings.quote: The economist Clara E. /məˈteɪi/, whose book this series follows
findings.problem: There is no id for "economist". It is supported by chapter 1's ledger, C1-01 ("Economist Clara E. Mattei..."), which page 13 doesn't cite. Page 13 also cites C2-XD02, which is about the 1920 Bank of England rise and isn't used on this page.

tested.summary:
Source: Clara E. Mattei, The Capital Order (2022).

Result: the combined script keeps every hard rule. I found no rule breaks. It has 5 should-fix and 7 minor wording problems, mostly words that mean two things and lines a first-time listener could mishear. All the fixes together add 12 words and about 6 seconds.

WHAT PASSED (checked line by line, plus the project's voice checker and sound scan, re-run in my folder):
- The money view is never named, and there is no "MMT". Mattei is written /məˈteɪi/. Ruhr no longer appears, because Germany was cut.
- No capitals for emphasis, no brackets, no exclamation marks. The only bracket should be the one accent line added at recording time.
- Every number and year is written as said. The only non-English letters are the three sound symbols in /məˈteɪi/.
- There are 28 "..." pauses, all at real turns in the sentence.
- Never used: "I" or "we", party politics, "cost" or "price" as a figure of speech, "unemployment", "central bank", "printing", bare "rates".
- Mattei's view is marked as hers twice ("She argues", "she says").
- Naomi Klein: none of her titles, coined phrases or near-copies. The only hits are two uses of "double", which is plain English and was already cleared in the voice brief. Her spirit is there: stakes on page 1, the viewer's own questions answered within a breath, landlords against families, people counted as people, and a closing pair of questions.
- Pinker: his principles without his manner. None of his habits ("to be sure", "consider", witty asides).
- Stock phrases: "It matters... because" (page 1) and "next time you hear the warning" (page 15) are familiar formulas, but each carries specific content, so keep them.
- The figures in the script's notes are right: about 24 spoken figures, sentences average 9 words, the longest is 19, and about 5,400 characters to send to the voice (5,439 with the accent line, about US$1).

ONE NAME PER THING: these are the swaps I found.
1. "banks" means two things: ordinary banks on page 9 ("sat in the banks") and banks like the Reserve Bank on page 13 ("Banks like our Reserve Bank").
2. "more people at the gate" (page 13) against "workers wait at the gate" (pages 3 and 11).
3. The noun "rise", used twice on page 14, against "go up" everywhere else.
4. "spending" (page 14) as a new name for "new money... spent".
5. Who creates new money: "the government" (page 1, the warning) against "the Reserve Bank" (page 2).

These are fine and need no change:
- "the cure" as a short form of "the usual cure";
- "more money" on pages 5 and 6, which describes an amount;
- "the money it had created" on page 8, which is Japan's whole amount and so a different thing;
- the job wording around "out of work";
- "the factory" used in general on pages 9 and 11.

Every other term is explained in plain words where it first appears, or is avoided.

LENGTH (140 words a minute, plus 0.6 seconds for each "..."):
- Spoken words: 886 when "twenty-one", "twenty-six" and "flat-out" count as the two words Malina says. The script's own count is 878, which counts them as one.
- Speech with pauses: about 6 minutes 37 seconds (6:33 on the 878 count).
- With 14 page turns, 3 guessing holds and the fade: about 7 minutes 11 seconds (7:07 on the 878 count). The script's own figure of 410 seconds (6:50) leaves out the pauses.
- At the recording's measured 164 words a minute, it comes to about 6 minutes in all.
- With every suggested fix applied: 898 spoken words, 30 pauses, about 6:43 of speech and about 7:17 in all. The voice checker and sound scan still find nothing.
