findings.quote: Spent on what? And who pays to stop it?
findings.problem: This is the line viewers carry away, and its "it" is unclear. "Spent on what?" is about the new money, so "stop it" can be heard as "stop the new money", which is the wrong idea. It could also attach to "the warning", the nearest noun. It also doesn't repeat page 12's question in the same words, so the refrain is lost.
findings.fix: "Spent on what? And who pays for the cure?" This is the same 6 words and says page 12's question again word for word. Change the card WHO PAYS TO STOP IT? to WHO PAYS FOR THE CURE?

findings.quote: The economist Clara E. /məˈteɪi/, whose book this series follows, disagrees. She argues that putting people out of work is how the cure works.
findings.problem: Two problems. First, the aside splits "The economist" from its verb "disagrees", which the teaching plan's rules for the ear forbid. Second, the disagreement can't be heard. Page 11 has already told viewers, as plain fact, that the cure works through fewer jobs ("hire fewer people... more workers wait at the gate"). So "she argues ... is how the cure works" sounds like something the film already said, and the listener test's question ("a fact, or someone's argument?") may fail.
findings.fix: "Clara E. /məˈteɪi/ is the economist whose book this series follows. She argues that putting people out of work isn't just unfortunate... it's how the cure works." This adds 3 words and 1 pause. It reuses the banks' own word, so the contrast can be heard. The claim is still the ledger's plain wording for C2-H18 ("works by putting people out of work"); the fact tester should confirm.

findings.quote: Banks like our Reserve Bank see putting people out of work as unfortunate... but not the goal.
findings.problem: The word "banks" names two different things. On page 9, "most of the new money just sat in the banks" means ordinary banks. Here, "Banks" means banks like the Reserve Bank. That breaks the one-name rule the other way round: one word for two things.
findings.fix: "Our Reserve Bank, and others like it, see putting people out of work as unfortunate... but not the goal." Leave page 9's everyday "the banks" alone. Card: OUR RESERVE BANK AND OTHERS LIKE IT: UNFORTUNATE, NOT THE GOAL.

findings.quote: Without the rise in petrol and diesel... two point nine.
findings.problem: This is a squeezed "what if" that a newcomer may not unpack: what was the price without what? It has no "percent", and the noun "rise" breaks the script's one name, "go up". The listener test's question 4 aims right at this line.
findings.fix: "If petrol and diesel prices hadn't gone up... two point nine percent." This adds 2 words. It is also closer to Stats NZ's own wording ("If petrol and diesel prices had not changed", from the second fact check).

findings.quote: Now new money is spent on what it makes.
findings.problem: The nearest noun before "it makes" is "new money", so the line can be heard as "what the money makes". This line sets up "whether it's spent... and on what" and "Spent on what?". Page 4 says it again: "The same new money is spent on what it makes."
findings.fix: "Now new money is spent on what the factory makes." Make the same change on page 4: "The same new money is spent on what the factory makes." That is 1 extra word in each place.

findings.quote: Where does new money come from? Here, the Reserve Bank can create it.
findings.problem: Straight after a question, "Here," can be heard as "Here's the answer" rather than "in New Zealand". The Reserve Bank is never introduced, although the teaching plan asked for it on page 2. Page 1 has just said the government creates new money, so a newcomer may wonder who actually does it.
findings.fix: "Here in New Zealand, our Reserve Bank can create it." This adds 3 words. "Our" is the script's own word for facts New Zealanders share.

findings.quote: With more people at the gate, she says, the workers inside have less power to ask for more pay.
findings.problem: This swaps the name in the picture's refrain. Pages 3 and 11 say "workers wait at the gate". This page says "people at the gate".
findings.fix: "With more workers waiting at the gate, she says, those inside have less power to ask for more pay." Still 19 words. "Those inside" avoids saying "workers" twice.

findings.quote: Homes worked like the flat-out factory too. Early in the war, crowds of war workers came to Glasgow, a British city.
findings.problem: The general idea comes before the scene. That goes against the rules' "a concrete case before each general idea" and Klein's habit of opening on the scene. "Homes worked" can also stumble on the ear, as if the homes did some work.
findings.fix: "Early in the war, crowds of war workers came to Glasgow, a British city. Its homes were like the flat-out factory too. With builders and materials gone to the war..." The word count stays about the same.

findings.quote: By November, about twenty thousand families were refusing to pay the extra.
findings.problem: With the year gone and only "Early in the war" before it, a listener who knows the war began in August 1914 will place this in November 1914. It was November 1915 (C2-XB01). This is a small date slip caused by the wording.
findings.fix: Either "By November nineteen fifteen, about twenty thousand families..." (2 more words and one more figure), or accept it knowingly. Ask the fact tester to decide.

findings.quote: That's a rise in costs... not in spending.
findings.problem: Two new names for the chapter's two causes arrive in the last 7 words: "rise" as a noun, and "spending". Everywhere else the cause is "new money... spent", and its effect "pushes prices up".
findings.fix: "That's costs pushing prices up... not spending." This uses the rule's own verb. Card: COSTS PUSHING PRICES UP / NOT SPENDING.

findings.quote: By the middle of twenty twenty-six, about a hundred and seventy thousand people were out of work.
findings.problem: This is the "who pays" page, where the voice brief wants the urgency, and it has no pause at all. The biggest number of people in the film gets no room to land. The voice brief asks for a pause after a number that needs to land.
findings.fix: "By the middle of twenty twenty-six... about a hundred and seventy thousand people were out of work." This adds 1 pause (0.6 s) and no words.

findings.quote: Businesses sell less, and hire fewer people.
findings.problem: "Businesses sell less" is a run of five s and z sounds in three words. A synthetic voice may blur it.
findings.fix: Listen for it in the take. If it blurs, use "Businesses sell less... and hire fewer people."

Counted the way this test asks (140 words a minute plus 0.6 s for each pause), it comes to about 7:07 to 7:11, not 6:50: 878 to 886 words, 393 to 397 s of speech, plus 34 s of page turns, holds and fade. final.title: Chapter 2 - what really causes inflation - for newcomers (revised after testing)
final.how_it_teaches:
Source: Clara E. Mattei, The Capital Order (2022). This is the combined newcomer script after three fresh testers read it: a simulated first-time listener panel, a fact checker and a rules-and-voice reader. I checked each finding against the ledger and the script before changing anything. Every confirmed must-fix and should-fix is applied, plus the cheap, safe minor ones. Nothing else changed.

THE SENTENCE A VIEWER SHOULD BE ABLE TO SAY BACK: whether new money pushes prices up depends on whether it's spent, and on what. When there are spare workers, materials and machines to make what it buys, it mostly gets more things made. When there aren't, it mostly pushes prices up. And the usual cure is paid for by people with loans and people out of work.

THE MODEL: two factories, each "a whole country... all its workers, materials and machines", set up before any real case.
- The quiet factory: machines still, workers waiting at the gate.
- The flat-out factory: "working as hard as they can".
- New money is "spent on what the factory makes".
- The rule is said the same way on pages 5 and 16: "When there are spare workers, materials and machines... new money, once it's spent, mostly gets more things made. When there aren't any spare... it mostly pushes prices up."

THE CASES, each placed on the picture out loud:
- Britain at war: "close to the flat-out factory". Millions were in uniform, ships were sunk, and the war was paid for partly with new money.
- Glasgow: "So for homes, Glasgow was like the flat-out factory". This is the first "on what" case. Landlords raised the rent and families refused to pay the extra, in neighbouring sentences.
- Japan: "most of it never reached the factory". Then the recap: "whether it's spent... and on what. Are there spare workers, materials and machines to make what it buys?"
- New Zealand 2020-21, the application check: the clue (about three in a hundred out of work, the lowest in more than thirty years), the guess, then a new answer page. It says "Close to the flat-out factory". Prices went up fast "partly from that, and partly from world prices, like oil". "The biggest push came from homes... building new ones, and rents", which is "on what" at home.
- The usual cure: "the flat-out factory slows... and more workers wait at the gate". Prices go up "more slowly. Not down".
- Who pays: rises "from late twenty twenty-one into twenty twenty-three", and "nearly six in a hundred" out of work by the middle of 2026, in the same unit as page 10. "The interest rate isn't the only reason for that."
- Two views that now clash: the banks call putting people out of work "unfortunate... but not the goal". Mattei "argues that putting people out of work is the main goal", marked "she argues" and "she says".
- The checkout: fuel makes almost everything made or moved cost more "in both factories", so "part of what you felt at the checkout wasn't new money being spent".

GUESSES AND RECAPS:
- Three guesses at page ends, each held about 4 seconds with an on-screen marker.
- The rule twice in the same words.
- "Whether it's spent... and on what" after Japan.
- The close: "Spent on what? And who pays for the cure?" (the second question repeats page 13 word for word).

ONE NAME FOR EACH THING: new money; the Reserve Bank ("Japan's version of our Reserve Bank", "Our Reserve Bank, and others like it"); out of work; the usual cure; interest rate; loans "cost more"; prices "go up"; workers "wait at the gate". There is no "rise", "unemployment", "central bank", bare "rates", "spending" or "printing".

VOICE: Naomi Klein in spirit only, never her words: stakes within 30 seconds, the viewer's own questions answered, who gains and who pays side by side, and urgency from facts. Pinker's principles, never his voice: a concrete scene before each idea, the imagined picture announced as imagined, each case's lesson said aloud, the picture's limits covered, and qualifications kept.

STILL CUT: Bank of England after 2008; Germany 1923; oil in 1973; Britain 1920; New Zealand house prices and the Royal Commission; the interest-rate figures; the 1-3% target; the review's "too strong, for too long". That last line is still the first one to bring back if there is room.

pages.name: The question
pages.text: You've felt it at the checkout. The same basket of shopping costs more than it did a year ago. That's inflation... prices in general, going up. Not one price tag. The whole basket. You've heard the warning too. If the government creates new money... prices will go up. Is that always true? It matters... because when prices go up too fast, the usual cure makes loans cost more. And that can put people out of work.
terms_explained: inflation (prices in general, going up; not one price tag, the whole basket)
the usual cure (makes loans cost more; explained in full on page 12)
pages.pictures: As in the combined version (page-1 reused with its two parts swapped, code only): the checkout, the basket and the tag from A YEAR AGO to NOW labelled EXAMPLE PRICES, then INFLATION / PRICES IN GENERAL, GOING UP and THE WHOLE BASKET. Then the chamber, where the invented politician (no party colours) mouths NEW MONEY → PRICES UP? and IS THAT ALWAYS TRUE?. The last card changes from BORROWING COSTS MORE to LOANS COST MORE → OUT OF WORK.

pages.name: Who can create new money
pages.text: Who can create new money? Here in New Zealand, the Reserve Bank can. It also tries to stop prices going up too fast. Economists who study how modern money works argue that a government like ours can't run out of its own money. But it can run out of workers, materials and machines.
terms_explained: who can create new money (the Reserve Bank 'can'; not the only source)
the Reserve Bank and what it tries to do (stop prices going up too fast)
economists who study how modern money works (their view, marked 'argue')
workers, materials and machines (the real limit)
pages.pictures: Code only. page-10's New Zealand street at dusk with a typed card THE RESERVE BANK (no logo) and a small CAN CREATE NEW MONEY, then TRIES TO STOP PRICES GOING UP TOO FAST. page-2's banknote bundles land: NEW MONEY. The card CAN'T RUN OUT OF ITS OWN MONEY / CAN RUN OUT OF... appears, then page-3's three cut-outs pop up: WORKERS / MATERIALS / MACHINES.

pages.name: The quiet factory
pages.text: Picture two factories. Think of each one as a whole country... all its workers, materials and machines. In the first, the machines stand still. Workers wait at the gate, hoping for a job. Call it the quiet factory. Now new money is spent on what the factory makes. The workers go in. The machines start. More things get made... and prices barely move.
terms_explained: the two-factories picture and what it stands for (a whole country's workers, materials and machines)
the quiet factory
new money spent on what the factory makes
pages.pictures: Unchanged. page-3's two-factories set, works A (code only), with the cards A WHOLE COUNTRY: WORKERS, MATERIALS, MACHINES and THE QUIET FACTORY. The queue waits at the gate and coins rain in: NEW MONEY SPENT. The workers go in, the windows light and goods come out. The price counter stays put, with a plain PRICES label.

pages.name: The flat-out factory (guess 1)
pages.text: In the second factory, every worker and every machine is already busy... working as hard as they can. No one waits at the gate. Call it the flat-out factory. The same new money is spent on what this factory makes. What do you think happens? Have a guess.
terms_explained: flat out (every worker and machine already busy, working as hard as they can)
the flat-out factory
pages.pictures: page-3's works B, gate empty, labelled THE FLAT-OUT FACTORY with a small line under it: FLAT OUT = WORKING AS HARD AS THEY CAN. The same coins rain in and the price counter freezes. WHAT HAPPENS? is held about 4 seconds, with a small on-screen marker that the film is waiting for a guess. Record it as the end of the page so the hold is real silence.

pages.name: The rule
pages.text: No spare workers, materials or machines... so no more things get made. Just more money, offered for the same things... and prices go up. Most economists agree on this much. So when there are spare workers, materials and machines... new money, once it's spent, mostly gets more things made. When there aren't any spare... it mostly pushes prices up.
terms_explained: spare
the rule, about new money once it's spent (recap 1, repeated on page 16)
pages.pictures: Code only. Works B's counter flips up. The three cut-outs return stamped NO SPARE, with MORE MONEY / SAME THINGS and a small MOST ECONOMISTS AGREE. Then a wide shot of both works with the rule cards SPARE → NEW MONEY, ONCE SPENT: MOSTLY MORE THINGS MADE and NONE SPARE → MOSTLY PRICES UP. This reuses the end of page-8 part A without YES, IT CAN or the card house.

pages.name: Britain at war
pages.text: Now a real case. Britain, during the First World War. Millions were in uniform. Soon, fewer than one worker in a hundred was out of work. German submarines sank ships carrying food and materials. And the war was paid for partly with new money. More money... and fewer things to buy. By the end of the war, prices had roughly doubled. Britain at war was close to the flat-out factory.
research_ids: Second fact check 12 Oct 2026 (early-1915 months just above 1%, hence 'soon'; Britain at war close to the second factory)
terms_explained: out of work (one worker in a hundred)
why workers weren't spare (millions in uniform)
the First World War (named)
pages.pictures: page-2's munitions hall with its words matched (code only): BRITAIN, FIRST WORLD WAR, then a typed card MILLIONS IN UNIFORM. The 100 dots with the last nearly empty: FEWER THAN 1 IN 100 OUT OF WORK. Then SHIPS SUNK: FOOD, MATERIALS; PARTLY NEW MONEY; MORE MONEY / FEWER THINGS; and the bars 1914 ×1 and 1918 ABOUT ×2. A quick cut to works B: CLOSE TO THE FLAT-OUT FACTORY.

pages.name: Glasgow's homes
pages.text: By nineteen fifteen, crowds of war workers had come to Glasgow, a British city, where homes were already short. With builders and materials gone to the war, few new homes were built. So for homes, Glasgow was like the flat-out factory. Landlords raised the rent... in places by up to a quarter. By November, about twenty thousand families were refusing to pay the extra. Within weeks, Britain's Parliament brought rents on small homes back to what they were before the war.
research_ids: Second fact check 12 Oct 2026 (1915 influx confirmed; house building virtually ceased; labour and materials went to the war; 'within weeks' counted from November)
terms_explained: a factory standing for one kind of thing ('for homes'), the first 'on what' case
homes already short, and few built while builders and materials were at the war
Britain's Parliament (so viewers don't picture Wellington)
pages.pictures: page-4's Glasgow tenement street (code only), titled GLASGOW 1915 (the year is now spoken) with HOMES ALREADY SHORT. Workers stream in. The building-site shot: BUILDERS AND MATERIALS GONE TO WAR / FEW NEW HOMES, with a tag FOR HOMES: LIKE THE FLAT-OUT FACTORY. Then RENT RAISED / UP TO +25% IN PLACES; rent strikers and the counter to 20,000 FAMILIES REFUSING THE EXTRA; and the stamp RENTS BACK TO BEFORE THE WAR. Never WON or RENTS FROZEN, and no Mary Barbour card.

pages.name: Japan, the guess (guess 2)
pages.text: Japan, twenty thirteen. Japan's version of our Reserve Bank set out to double the money it had created... in two years. If the warning is right, prices should go up fast. What do you think happened? Have a guess.
terms_explained: Japan's version of our Reserve Bank (makes sense now that page 2 has said what ours does)
pages.pictures: Unchanged. page-5 part A's noodle counter at night: JAPAN 2013. The stack of invented notes doubles: ×2 MONEY / IN TWO YEARS. During the hold of about 4 seconds, the dashed line, labelled IF THE WARNING IS RIGHT, climbs under WHAT HAPPENED?

pages.name: Japan, the answer
pages.text: Prices barely moved. For about eight years, they went up about half a percent a year, on average. Why? One reason economists give... most of the new money just sat in the banks. In our picture, most of it never reached the factory. So it's not just how much new money there is. It's whether it's spent... and on what. Are there spare workers, materials and machines to make what it buys?
terms_explained: money that is created but not spent (sat in the banks, never reached the factory)
recap 2: whether it's spent, and on what
what 'on what' asks: are there spare workers, materials and machines to make what it buys
pages.pictures: Code only. The real line drawn almost level: ABOUT ½% A YEAR. Coins pile up in front of page-9's card bank beside works A and never reach the yard: MOST SAT IN THE BANKS. The card NOT JUST HOW MUCH / WHETHER IT'S SPENT, AND ON WHAT, then one more typed card: SPARE WORKERS, MATERIALS, MACHINES TO MAKE WHAT IT BUYS?

pages.name: New Zealand, the guess (guess 3, an application check)
pages.text: Now, here. When Covid hit in twenty twenty, the Reserve Bank created new money. And the government spent more... including help with wages. By the end of twenty twenty-one, almost everyone looking for work had found it. Only about three in a hundred were out of work... the lowest in more than thirty years. Which factory was New Zealand closer to? Have a guess.
research_ids: Second fact check 12 Oct 2026 (lowest since the count began in 1986; almost no unemployment in the 1950s-60s)
terms_explained: out of work as a share (about three in a hundred)
what part of the government's money went on (help with wages)
almost everyone looking for work had found it (so low joblessness isn't heard as bad)
pages.pictures: page-8 part B's New Zealand street (code only): NEW ZEALAND 2020. Notes land (NEW MONEY), with the card GOVERNMENT SPENT MORE / INCLUDING HELP WITH WAGES. Then 2021, with the 100-dot panel showing 3 empty dots: ABOUT 3 IN 100 OUT OF WORK / LOWEST IN 30+ YEARS, credited to Stats NZ. Then a wide shot of both factories with WHICH ONE?, held about 4 seconds. No card house, no +30% and no review desk.

pages.name: New Zealand, the answer (new page)
pages.text: Close to the flat-out factory. Almost no one was waiting at the gate. And prices here went up fast... partly from that, and partly from world prices, like oil. The biggest push came from homes... building new ones, and rents.
terms_explained: none new: the outcome is said, with both causes ('partly... and partly')
homes as the biggest push (building costs and rents, not house prices), 'on what' at home
pages.pictures: Code only, no new paintings. A quick cut to works B with the gate almost empty: CLOSE TO THE FLAT-OUT FACTORY. Then PRICES WENT UP FAST, splitting into PARTLY: FEW SPARE and PARTLY: WORLD PRICES, LIKE OIL (page-7 part A's oil barrel, no counter). Then page-4's building-site shot relabelled NEW ZEALAND: BIGGEST PUSH: BUILDING NEW HOMES, AND RENTS. No house-price figures, no +30%, no review desk.

pages.name: The usual cure
pages.text: So what's the usual cure? The Reserve Bank raises its interest rate. Interest is the extra you pay back when you borrow. Many loans cost more... so people have less to spend. Businesses sell less, and hire fewer people. And prices go up more slowly. Not down... just more slowly. In our picture, the flat-out factory slows... and more workers wait at the gate.
terms_explained: interest (the extra you pay back when you borrow) and interest rate
the usual cure, in full
bringing inflation down means prices go up more slowly, not down
pages.pictures: Code only, as before without the opening CLOSE TO THE FLAT-OUT FACTORY cut (now on page 11). page-10 part A's dial relabelled INTEREST RATE, its needle rising with no figures, and INTEREST = THE EXTRA YOU PAY BACK. Coins are pulled back into the card bank (LOANS COST MORE) and a shop light goes out (LESS TO SPEND), then FEWER HIRED and PRICES GO UP MORE SLOWLY / NOT DOWN. On works B the smoke thins and the queue returns: MORE WORKERS AT THE GATE.

pages.name: Who pays, here
pages.text: Who pays for the cure? From late twenty twenty-one into twenty twenty-three, the Reserve Bank raised its interest rate again and again. Loans cost more, and jobs got harder to find. By the middle of twenty twenty-six... nearly six in a hundred were out of work. The interest rate isn't the only reason for that.
terms_explained: none new: the share out of work is in the same unit as page 10 (three in a hundred, then nearly six)
pages.pictures: page-10 part A: the dial climbs in steps, LATE 2021 TO 2023: AGAIN AND AGAIN, with no rate figures. page-10's 100-dot panel returns with nearly 6 empty dots: NEARLY 6 IN 100 OUT OF WORK, credited STATS NZ, MIDDLE OF 2026, with a small NOT THE ONLY REASON. The ABOUT 170,000 card, the 1920/1921 bars and the 3.2%→5.6% counter are removed.

pages.name: Two views
pages.text: Our Reserve Bank, and others like it, see putting people out of work as unfortunate... but not the goal. Clara E. /məˈteɪi/ is the economist whose book this series follows. She argues that putting people out of work is the main goal. With more workers waiting at the gate, she says, those inside have less power to ask for more pay.
research_ids: C2-XD02 (background only: her view is contested)
terms_explained: who Mattei is (the economist whose book this series follows)

pages.pictures: page-9 part B (code only). A typed card OUR RESERVE BANK AND OTHERS LIKE IT: UNFORTUNATE, NOT THE GOAL (no quotation marks). Her book with CLARA E. MATTEI, THE CAPITAL ORDER (2022), and MATTEI ARGUES: THE MAIN GOAL. The queue at the gate grows and the iron weight drops on the pay packet: LESS POWER TO ASK FOR MORE PAY. No portrait.

pages.name: Back at the checkout
pages.text: And the checkout? In the year to June twenty twenty-six, prices here went up four point one percent. If petrol and diesel prices hadn't changed... prices would have gone up two point nine percent. When fuel like that costs more, almost everything that's made or moved costs more... in both factories. So part of what you felt at the checkout wasn't new money being spent.

pages.name: Spent on what?
pages.text: Does new money always push prices up? No. When there are spare workers, materials and machines... new money, once it's spent, mostly gets more things made. When there aren't any spare... it mostly pushes prices up. So next time you hear the warning... ask two questions. Spent on what? And who pays for the cure?
